query: What was the study's primary aim and hypothesis about lean body mass and protein dose?
reference_answer: The study compared muscle protein synthesis (MPS) after 20 or 40 g of whey protein following whole-body resistance exercise in resistance-trained men with lower or higher lean body mass. The authors hypothesized that men with higher lean body mass would need more protein for maximal MPS stimulation.

evidence.quote: The primary aim of the present study was to determine the response of MPS to two different doses of protein following a bout of whole-body resistance exercise in resistance-trained males with a large amount of LBM compared to those with a smaller amount of LBM.
We hypothesized that the group with higher LBM would require more protein for maximal stimulation of MPS during recovery from whole-body resistance exercise compared with the group with lower LBM.

query: How were participants selected and divided into the lower- and higher-lean-body-mass groups?
reference_answer: Thirty healthy, resistance-trained men were studied. Those with lean body mass (LBM) of 65 kg or less formed the lower-LBM group (LLBM, n=15), and those with LBM of 70 kg or more formed the higher-LBM group (HLBM, n=15); volunteers between those thresholds were excluded.

evidence.quote: Thirty healthy, resistance-trained (≥2 sessions per week for previous 6 months) males participated in the present study and were grouped according to LBM.
those that possessed LBM ≤ 65 kg were categorized as the lower lean body mass (LLBM) group (n = 15) and LBM ≥ 70 kg were categorized as the higher lean body mass (HLBM) group (n = 15).
Volunteers with LBM between these values were not eligible to participate in the present study.

query: What was the randomized crossover intervention used to compare the two protein doses?
reference_answer: Each participant completed two randomized, double-blind infusion trials about two weeks apart. Immediately after whole-body exercise, participants drank either 20 or 40 g of whey-protein isolate in 500 mL of water, with the order randomized and the drinks prepared by an independent investigator.

evidence.quote: In a two-group, randomized, double-blind, crossover design, each volunteer participated in two infusion trials designed to measure the response of MPS following whole-body resistance exercise and whey protein ingestion.
Each infusion trial included the ingestion of either 20 or 40 g of whey protein isolate
The order of infusion trials, and thus dose of ingested protein, was randomized and an independent investigator prepared the drinks.

query: How was the whole-body resistance exercise and post-exercise sampling protocol performed?
reference_answer: About one hour after tracer infusion began, participants exercised in the order chest press, latissimus pull-down, leg curl, leg press, and leg extension at 75% of one-repetition maximum. They performed three sets of 10 repetitions plus a fourth set to volitional failure. A 20- or 40-g drink was consumed immediately afterward, and muscle biopsies were collected at 0, 180, and 300 minutes with repeated arterialized blood sampling through 300 minutes.

evidence.quote: Approximately 1 h after starting the infusion participants performed an acute bout of resistance exercise on the following machines in the following order; chest press, latissimus pull-down, leg curl, leg press, and leg extension.
Participants worked at 75% of their 1 RM at a cadence of 1 sec concentric - 2 sec eccentric contraction.
Each participant was instructed to complete three sets of 10 repetitions with a final fourth set to volitional failure
Participants then consumed a drink that contained either 20 or 40 g of a whey protein isolate made up in 500mL of water
Subsequent muscle biopsies were obtained from the same leg at 180 and 300min.

query: Which participant characteristics differed significantly between the lower- and higher-LBM groups?
reference_answer: The higher-LBM group had greater body mass, height, lean body mass, appendicular lean mass, and right- and left-leg press one-repetition maximum. Age, fat mass, lean-mass percentage, and fat-mass percentage were not marked as significantly different.

evidence.quote: Appendicular lean mass (kg) | 28.1 ± 2.1 | 37.4 ± 2.3*
1RM leg press (right leg) (kg) | 126.0 ± 21.8 | 159.0 ± 29.5*
1RM leg press (left leg) (kg) | 123.6 ± 23.9 | 158.7 ± 29.1*
*Significant difference from LLBM (P < 0.05).

query: What does Figure 1 summarize about the infusion trial?
reference_answer: Figure 1 is the schematic of the infusion trial: participants underwent fasting, tracer infusion, whole-body resistance exercise, immediate ingestion of either 20 or 40 g whey protein, and serial blood and muscle sampling through 300 minutes.

evidence.quote: A schematic diagram of the experimental protocol is presented in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Schematic diagram of infusion trial protocol.

query: How did the two protein doses affect plasma leucine concentrations?
reference_answer: Plasma leucine peaked at 45 minutes after 20 g and at 60 minutes after 40 g. The 40-g dose produced higher leucine concentrations at several early time points and a larger 0–300-minute leucine area under the curve than 20 g.

evidence.quote: Plasma leucine concentrations peaked at 45 min with 20 g of ingested whey protein and at 60 min with 40 g in both groups

Plasma leucine concentrations were higher at 45 (d=1.81; CI=1.21-2.42), 60 (d=3.13; CI=2.38-3.89), 90 (d=2.64; CI=1.94-3.33) and 120 min (d = 2; CI = 1.38-2.63) in both groups with 40 g compared with 20 g of whey protein
Plasma leucine concentrations, expressed as AUC after protein ingestion, were greater with 40g

query: What did the intracellular amino-acid measurements show for the two doses?
reference_answer: Muscle intracellular leucine was higher after 40 g than 20 g at both 180 and 300 minutes, and its area under the curve was also higher with 40 g. Intracellular phenylalanine did not differ between doses or groups and declined at 180 and 300 minutes relative to baseline.

evidence.quote: Muscle IC leucine concentrations were greater with 40 g compared with 20 g at 180 (d = 0.57; CI = 0.05-1.09) and 300 min (d = 0.65; CI = 0.13-1.17)
IC leucine concentrations, expressed as AUC, were greater with 40 g than 20 g
There were no differences between groups or doses in IC phenylalanine concentrations (Table 3).
IC phenylalanine concentrations were lower at 180 and 300 min compared with 0 min

query: How did protein dose affect phenylalanine oxidation and plasma urea?
reference_answer: Phenylalanine oxidation was higher with 40 g than 20 g at 60 and 90 minutes, and its 0–300-minute area under the curve was also higher. Plasma urea was higher with 40 g from 120 through 300 minutes and had a higher area under the curve.

evidence.quote: The rate of phenylalanine oxidation was greater with ingestion of 40 g compared with 20 g of ingested whey protein at 60 (d = 1.35; CI = 0.78-1.91) and 90 min (d = 1.51; CI=0.93-2.08)
Phenylalanine oxidation rates, expressed as AUC, were greater with ingestion of 40 g of whey protein

Plasma urea concentrations were greater with ingestion of 40 g of whey protein compared with 20 g at 120 (d=0.66; CI=0.14-1.18), 180 (d=0.55; CI=0.03-1.06), 240 (d=0.66; CI=0.14-1.18), and 300min (d=0.58; CI=0.07-1.10)
The AUC for plasma urea concentrations was greater in 40g

query: How was myofibrillar fractional synthesis rate (FSR) calculated, and which precursor enrichment was used?
reference_answer: FSR was calculated with the standard precursor–product equation from the change in bound phenylalanine enrichment divided by intracellular phenylalanine enrichment and tracer-incorporation time. Intracellular phenylalanine enrichment was the precursor for all FSR calculations.

EIC is the IC phenylalanine enrichment of the biopsies and t is time of tracer incorporation (h).
IC phenylalanine enrichment was used as the precursor in all FSR calculations.

query: What was the main finding for myofibrillar MPS when 40 g was compared with 20 g of protein?
reference_answer: Across both LBM groups, 40 g of whey protein produced about 20% higher myofibrillar FSR than 20 g during the 0–300-minute recovery period after whole-body resistance exercise. There was no significant protein-dose-by-LBM-group interaction.

evidence.quote: There was no significant interaction between protein dose and LBM group
Overall, myofibrillar FSR was ~20% higher with ingestion of 40 g compared with 20 g of whey protein
Overall (groups combined), MPS was stimulated to a greater extent following ingestion of 40 g

query: Was the higher FSR with 40 g confined to an early part of recovery?
reference_answer: No. The 40-g dose produced significantly higher FSR in both the early 0–180-minute interval and the later 180–300-minute interval, indicating a similar dose pattern across both periods.

evidence.quote: FSR was significantly greater for 40 g compared with 20 g at both the early (0-180 min) and later (180-300 min) time periods following protein ingestion.

query: How did p70S6K1 activity compare with the MPS response?
reference_answer: Protein dose did not change p70S6K1 activity, although activity was higher in the LLBM group and rose at 180 minutes relative to baseline. Thus, the signaling response did not mirror the significantly greater MPS observed with 40 g.

evidence.quote: There was no effect of protein dose on p70S6K1 activity
There were no differences in p70S6K1 activity between the 20 and 40 g trials in the present study, yet there was a significant difference in MPS between protein doses.
p70S6K1 activity was 1.6-fold greater at 180 min following protein ingestion in the LLBM compared with the HLBM group.

query: What mechanism did the authors propose for why 40 g outperformed 20 g after whole-body exercise?
reference_answer: The authors proposed that whole-body exercise activates more muscle and therefore creates a greater overall amino-acid demand. With only 20 g, amino-acid supply may be insufficient for the exercised muscles, whereas 40 g provides more amino acids across those muscles; this explanation remains a proposal rather than a definitive demonstration.

evidence.quote: the greater the amount of muscle utilized during a resistance exercise bout, the greater the demand for amino acids that must be met by exogenous sources
We propose that amino acid supply may have been insufficient with ingestion of 20 g whey protein to meet the demands of the exercised muscle during recovery from whole-body resistance exercise.

Although we believe the amount of muscle exercised is the most likely explanation for the differences in results observed between this study and previous studies (Moore et al. 2009; Witard et al. 2014), alternative nonphysiological explanations must be considered.

query: What limitations did the authors state about generalization and identifying a maximal protein dose?
reference_answer: The findings are limited to healthy, young, resistance-trained individuals, and older or other populations may respond differently. Because the study tested only 20 and 40 g, it cannot identify the dose that maximally stimulates MPS; further studies are needed, including studies of whether the maximal dose depends on LBM.

evidence.quote: our results are limited to healthy, young resistance-trained individuals. Other populations with differing metabolic responses to protein, for example, older individuals (Moore et al. 2015), may respond differently.
it is not possible to determine the dose of protein necessary to stimulate a maximal MPS response from our data. We examined the MPS response to two amounts of protein only.

Further study is required to identify a maximal stimulatory protein dose for MPS following whole-body resistance exercise and to explore if this maximal dose is influenced by LBM in different populations.
